title: Project 2: number guessing game
learningObjectives: Define the number-guessing game's rules, target range, attempt limit, feedback and replay behaviour before implementing the program.
Generate a pseudo-random target using rand and seed the generator once with srand, while explaining why this mechanism is not suitable for security-sensitive randomness.
Read complete input lines with fgets and parse guesses with strtol, checking conversion, range errors, trailing characters and allowed target bounds.
Implement low, high and correct feedback, a bounded attempt counter, invalid-input handling and a clear win/loss outcome.
Separate game-round logic, target generation, input parsing and replay interaction into functions that can be tested independently.
Test deterministic game scenarios, boundary guesses, attempt exhaustion, malformed input, EOF and replay behaviour using strict C11 builds.

understand.concept: A number guessing game chooses a secret integer within a documented range, accepts guesses and gives feedback until the player finds the target or reaches an attempt limit. This project uses the inclusive range 1 through 100 and allows seven valid guesses per round. A guess below the target receives “Too low”; a guess above it receives “Too high”; an equal guess wins. Invalid lines and out-of-range numbers are rejected without consuming an attempt. The game can offer another round after a win or loss.
understand.whyItMatters: The project combines loops, decisions, counters, pseudo-random number generation, robust text input, functions and state transitions. It also teaches an important distinction: a simple game can use rand for non-security purposes, but predictable pseudo-random generators must not be used for passwords, tokens, gambling systems or security decisions.
understand.analogy: Imagine a person choosing a number from a range and giving clues after each guess. The clues narrow the possible range, while a fixed number of turns makes the game a bounded process.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not make rand truly random. rand produces a deterministic pseudo-random sequence from an internal state. The sequence can be repeatable and its quality and range are implementation-dependent.

keyTerms.definition: A value generated by a deterministic algorithm that is designed to look irregular for ordinary uses.
A standard C library function that returns a pseudo-random integer from 0 through RAND_MAX.
A standard C library function that sets the seed used by rand; seed once for a run, not before every draw.
The initial state used to start a pseudo-random sequence; the same seed repeats the same sequence for a given implementation.
Using a remainder such as rand() % 100 to map a value into a smaller range; it can introduce modulo bias unless the source range is an exact multiple.
The maximum number of valid guesses allowed in one round.
Checking that the complete input line contains a valid integer within the permitted range.

gameRules.detail: Seven valid guesses per round; invalid input does not consume a guess.
Report Too low, Too high or Correct after each valid guess.
Win when the target is guessed; otherwise reveal the target after the seventh valid incorrect guess.
Accept one integer per line; reject blank, malformed, trailing-text and out-of-range input.
After a round, accept y to play again or n to exit; EOF exits gracefully.

understand.history: Games based on guessing hidden numbers are common exercises for teaching loops and conditional logic. C's rand and srand are defined by the standard library for simple pseudo-random sequences. The same seed repeats the sequence for a given implementation, making seeded runs useful for debugging. For robust testing, the project will also inject a fixed target into the game logic rather than depending on a random value.

explain.narrative:
Separate the game into small responsibilities. A target generator chooses an integer in the documented range. A parser converts one input line into a valid guess. A round function compares the guess with the target, updates the attempt count and reports win or loss. The main function handles replay and program exit.

Seed the pseudo-random generator once near program startup with srand((unsigned)time(NULL)). Do not call srand before every guess: reseeding repeatedly with a clock that has coarse resolution can produce repeated values. rand returns a value between zero and RAND_MAX. Mapping it with rand() % 100 + 1 is simple for a beginner game, but it may have a small modulo bias when the number of possible rand values is not divisible by 100. rand is not cryptographically secure and must not be used for security tokens or other security-sensitive choices.

Read a complete line with fgets, then use strtol to parse an integer. Reset errno before conversion; verify that at least one digit was consumed, reject ERANGE, skip trailing whitespace and require the rest of the line to be empty. Finally check that the number is between 1 and 100. This rejects inputs such as an empty line, 25abc, 2.5, a huge integer and 0. Invalid input should not consume one of the seven valid attempts.

The first example keeps the game round deterministic by passing a fixed target to the round function. Its test harness checks low, high, correct, invalid and attempt-limit scenarios without depending on randomness or terminal input. The second example is a complete interactive game. It seeds rand once, reads and validates guesses, offers low/high clues, enforces the attempt limit and asks whether to replay. It exits cleanly on EOF. The target generator uses rand only for this non-security game.

examples.title: Test a deterministic guessing round
examples.explanation: game_init establishes a known initial state and rejects targets outside 1 through 100. game_guess rejects invalid guesses and calls after the round has finished; only valid guesses increment attempts. A correct guess marks the round finished and won. The test harness injects known targets so it can test low, high, correct, lower and upper boundaries, invalid target setup and attempt exhaustion deterministically. The game logic does not call rand, which makes the core state transitions straightforward to test. A complete interface could distinguish invalid input from a guess after the attempt limit with a richer result type; this compact example keeps the focus on the game state.

examples.title: Build the complete interactive number guessing game
examples.explanation: read_line uses fgets with a fixed-size buffer, detects overlong input and discards the remainder so it cannot become a second input line. parse_guess uses strtol, checks that at least one digit was read, rejects ERANGE, skips trailing whitespace and requires a value from 1 through 100. Invalid input does not consume an attempt. play_round accepts at most seven valid guesses and returns false only when input reaches EOF. make_target maps rand into the game's 1-to-100 range; srand is called once in main. Modulo mapping can be slightly biased, and rand is predictable and not secure. The replay loop accepts y or n and exits on EOF or an unrecognised response. For deterministic automated tests, use the first example's injected target rather than expecting a particular time-seeded random number.

practise.guidedTask: Run the deterministic tests with target 37 and trace guesses 20, 50 and 37. Record the feedback and attempt count after each guess. Then use targets 1 and 100 to test the range boundaries, and target 60 to exhaust all seven attempts without winning.
practise.independentTask: Extend the interactive game with a difficulty selection: easy (1–50, 8 guesses), normal (1–100, 7 guesses) and hard (1–500, 9 guesses). Keep the target generator and round logic separate. Add a deterministic test mode that accepts a fixed target and test empty input, malformed numbers, trailing text, out-of-range guesses, overlong lines, EOF, attempt exhaustion and replay. Explain the limits of rand and modulo mapping.
hints: Seed rand once at program startup; reseeding before each guess can repeat values when the clock has coarse resolution.
Use a fixed target in unit tests so low, high, correct and attempt-limit behaviour is repeatable.
Check strtol's end pointer and errno, then reject trailing non-whitespace characters and values outside 1 through 100.
Decide whether invalid input consumes an attempt; this project's rule is that only valid in-range guesses count.
The expression rand() % 100 + 1 is simple but can have modulo bias; rand is not appropriate for security-sensitive randomness.
Test both target boundaries, the final allowed attempt, one guess after the limit, EOF and replay input.

questions.prompt: When should srand be called in this number guessing game?
options: Once near program startup before generating targets
Before every guess
After every incorrect guess
Only after the player wins
questions.answer: Once near program startup before generating targets
questions.explanation: Seeding once starts the pseudo-random sequence. Repeated reseeding, especially with a coarse clock, can repeat values.

options: A pseudo-random integer from 0 through RAND_MAX
A cryptographically secure password
A guaranteed value from 1 through 100
A floating-point value between 0 and 1
questions.answer: A pseudo-random integer from 0 through RAND_MAX
questions.explanation: The C standard library rand function returns an integer in the inclusive range zero to RAND_MAX.

questions.prompt: Why does parse_guess check the end pointer returned by strtol?
options: To ensure the input contains a number and no unexpected trailing text
To seed the random number generator
To count how many attempts remain
To sort the guesses
questions.answer: To ensure the input contains a number and no unexpected trailing text
questions.explanation: The end pointer shows where conversion stopped; after skipping whitespace, the parser requires the rest of the line to be empty.

questions.prompt: According to this project's rules, does an invalid or out-of-range input consume a guess?
options: No, only a valid integer from 1 through 100 consumes an attempt
Yes, every line always consumes an attempt
Only blank input consumes an attempt
Only text input consumes two attempts
questions.answer: No, only a valid integer from 1 through 100 consumes an attempt
questions.explanation: The attempt counter increments only after parsing and range validation succeed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about rand is correct?
options: It is predictable pseudo-randomness and is not suitable for security-sensitive choices
It is guaranteed to be cryptographically secure
It produces a perfectly uniform value for every modulo range
It does not need a seed
questions.answer: It is predictable pseudo-randomness and is not suitable for security-sensitive choices
questions.explanation: rand is intended for simple pseudo-random sequences, not security tokens or adversarial settings; modulo mapping may also introduce bias.
